A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LoRA-MCL research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, references, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the substantial revision.

before.justification: v1 reports original Markov-chain simulations and experiments on AudioCaps, Clotho-V2, TextCaps, and an artificial bilingual captioning dataset.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds machine-translation experiments, baseline comparisons, relaxation ablations, and quantitative specialization analyses.

M1.justification: v1 uses fixed-epsilon relaxed WTA and proposes annealing as future work. v2 implements an additional annealed variant with likelihood-dependent hypothesis weights and a decreasing temperature schedule (Section 3.3). This extends the training objective while retaining the multiple-LoRA architecture and parallel execution.

E1.justification: The captioning datasets, bilingual captioning scenario, and Markov mixtures are retained. v2 adds a distinct text-only translation task: English–German parallel training using WMT’17–20 and Flores-200 data, followed by English-to-German evaluation on the multi-reference newstest2014 subset (Section 5.4 and Appendix E.8).

E2.justification: Beyond the retained LoRA-MLE comparisons, v2 evaluates LoRA-MoE with conventional and stochastic-router decoding, audio test-time augmentation, multi-head MCL alternatives, DAC-RLD on audio captioning, and PaliGemma-3B on TextCaps. Their participation is documented in Tables 6–12, substantially broadening the comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 introduces translation evaluation with 500 inputs, ten references each, and Loo-BLEU/Pairwise-BLEU, plus a 70/30 SVM probe split. Table 1 changes the hypothesis/rank grid. The stated TextCaps setup changes from AdamW, beta2=0.98, peak learning rate 1e-4, and warmup 0.1 to Adam, beta2=0.999, 2e-4, and 0.03. These are reported setting revisions; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v1 already examines epsilon, hypothesis count, and bilingual specialization. v2 substantially extends epsilon sensitivity, adds temperature-decay and multi-head initialization ablations (Tables 5–6), introduces PCA/SVM specialization probes (Figure 6 and Appendix E.7.4), and adds qualitative examples across tasks. The earlier three- and four-candidate audio quality–diversity plots are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations across three training seeds for the Markov-chain experiment. v2 adds no corresponding repeated-run information, confidence intervals, or significance testing for the captioning, translation, or specialization results.

E6.justification: Audio results are extensively revised: Table 1’s retained K=5 AudioCaps/Clotho losses change from 1.927/2.629 to 1.999/2.643. Numerous baseline, annealing, translation, and specialization results are added, while some configurations and Div-1 results disappear. Existing TextCaps and bilingual scores are largely retained. Sampling results switch from fixed-epsilon MCL to annealed MCL, so those are replacement results under different conditions.

T1.justification: The principal entropy bounds, mixture assumptions, and Markov-chain results remain. Appendix B newly qualifies the gradient-update convergence argument, stating that strict monotonicity requires additional learning-rate and smoothness assumptions. Appendix E.6.2 also derives the relaxed-loss decomposition and the epsilon=(K−1)/K threshold where its competitive term vanishes.

C1.justification: v2 adds a general-purpose software package as an explicit abstract-level deliverable and extends the stated empirical contribution to machine translation. The central claims about adapting MCL through LoRA, capturing mixture modes, and obtaining a favorable quality–diversity trade-off remain.

C2.justification: v2 explains large-epsilon homogenization and slow-annealing failures through critical-temperature behavior, and extends the limitations discussion to both relaxation variants. It revises the sampling interpretation to distinguish AudioCaps from Clotho and explicitly qualifies the PaliGemma comparison because that model underwent full-weight fine-tuning. The basic mode-specialization interpretation is retained.

D1.justification: v1 promises future code release; v2 reports available code and a general-purpose package and supplies a repository link. The appendices add audio input formatting and loss-token boundaries, adapter/router initialization, annealing settings, metric libraries and tokenizers, and translation implementation details. Reported total computation increases from approximately 20,000 to 25,000 GPU hours.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands engagement with LoRA-MoE, test-time augmentation, diverse translation, DAC-RLD, and PaliGemma literature. It replaces v1’s assertion that MoE routing makes it incompatible with MCL with discussion of LoRA-based MoE adaptations and uncertain expert specialization. The appendix also develops explicit positioning against prior captioning systems.

P1.justification: The main text is extensively condensed and rewritten. The parallelization mathematics moves into Appendix E.5, while Appendix E is reorganized into dedicated metrics, training, decoding, ablation, and task-specific sections with expanded explanations. A detailed appendix table of contents improves navigation.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout. v2 adds an architecture diagram, translation plot, PCA plot, and several comparison/ablation tables; redesigns the audio comparison plot and legends; and rearranges existing bilingual displays and tables. The earlier three- and four-candidate audio plots are removed, and several tables change their displayed columns.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1’s narrow comparator base and largely untested multi-head rationale through direct alternative-method comparisons, initialization controls, and broader collapse analyses. Quantitative specialization probes and text-only translation strengthen the evidence for the proposed mechanism and applicability, while expanded implementation information improves reproducibility. Some audio-score revisions remain unexplained, and revised TextCaps settings accompany retained scores, limiting cross-version performance conclusions. The substantial improvement rests on stronger validation and documentation.
